title: inspect: CreateContainerConfigError (runAsNonRoot vs root image) misclassified as image_pull_other
body:
## Summary

A pod failing with `CreateContainerConfigError` caused by a securityContext violation
(`runAsNonRoot: true` against a root image) is classified as **`image_pull_other`** — a cause
code asserting a registry/network failure. The image had in fact been pulled successfully, and
the cluster said so in an event that `inspect` also had available.

Two separate problems: the misclassification itself, and the absence of any cause code that
actually fits this failure.

## Environment

- crashcause `v0.1.0` (`GitCommit 8a4a6fff`), installed via `kubectl krew install --manifest`
- `darwin/arm64`
- k3s v1.x via k3d, single node, local

## Reproduce

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: runasnonroot-repro
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true          # and no runAsUser to reconcile it
  containers:
    - name: nginx-proxy
      image: nginx:alpine       # image declares USER root (UID 0)
```

```
kubectl crashcause inspect runasnonroot-repro -n default
```

## Actual

```
default/... container nginx-proxy — image_pull_other (medium confidence)

  The kubelet could not pull the image for container "nginx-proxy", and the registry error is
  neither an authorization failure nor a missing image. Typical causes are a network timeout,
  a TLS/proxy problem, or a registry rate limit or quota.

  Evidence:
    - waiting reason: CreateContainerConfigError
    - image: nginx:alpine
    - event: Failed (x8480): Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root
```

`--verbose` shows a second rule matched at the same confidence:

```
  also matched: config_missing_reference (medium) — The kubelet could not create container
  "nginx-proxy": CreateContainerConfigError means a referenced ConfigMap, Secret or key could
  not be resolved. The container never started.
```

## Expected

A cause code describing a securityContext / container-config rejection. Not an image-pull code —
and specifically not one whose explanation names causes ("network timeout", "registry rate
limit") that are all falsifiable from data `inspect` already fetched.

## What actually happened in the cluster

```
1. kubelet pulls nginx:alpine                → SUCCEEDS
   event  Pulled x8479  "Container image \"nginx:alpine\" already present on machine"
2. kubelet reads the image config to create the container
   image declares USER root; pod demands runAsNonRoot with no runAsUser override
3. kubelet REFUSES to create the container
   waiting.reason  = CreateContainerConfigError
   waiting.message = "container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root"
   event  Failed x8480
4. retry forever
```

Verified from the live cluster:

```
$ kubectl get pod ... -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext}'
{"runAsNonRoot":true}

$ kubectl get pod ... -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].state}'
{"waiting":{"message":"container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root ...",
            "reason":"CreateContainerConfigError"}}

$ kubectl get events -n default --field-selector involvedObject.name=... \
    -o custom-columns=REASON:.reason,COUNT:.count,MSG:.message
Failed   8480   Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root ...
Pulled   8479   Container image "nginx:alpine" already present on machine
```

This is a kubelet pre-start config check occurring *strictly after* a successful pull. The
container never starts, so `RESTARTS` stays 0 while the event counters climb into the thousands.

## Analysis

I haven't read the source, so the following is inferred from observable behaviour — but the
output is fairly specific about where it goes wrong.

**1. Classification appears keyed on the event reason, which is overloaded.** The kubelet emits
`reason=Failed` for image-pull failures, container-*create* failures and container-*start*
failures alike. Any rule predicated on `event.reason == Failed` matches all three families.
Kubernetes exposes a precise discriminator for this — `containerStatuses[].state.waiting.reason`
(`ErrImagePull` / `ImagePullBackOff` / `CreateContainerConfigError` / `CreateContainerError` /
`CrashLoopBackOff`).

**2. `image_pull_other` is the pull family's fallback, so it has the family's weakest predicate.**
`image_pull_auth` and `image_pull_not_found` look message-keyed (`unauthorized`, `manifest
unknown`); the runAsNonRoot message matches neither, so it falls through to the catch-all. The
bucket intended for "a pull error I can't attribute" is effectively serving as "any `Failed`
event I can't attribute".

**3. The waiting reason is gathered as evidence but is not part of the predicate.** The report
cites `waiting reason: CreateContainerConfigError` *in support of* an image-pull verdict, and
quotes the true cause verbatim on the next line. The field is decoration in the output rather
than a discriminator in the rule. The disproof was in the same event list the "proof" came from:
a successful `Pulled` event refutes the whole `image_pull_*` family outright.

**4. The tie-break favours the fallback.** Both rules scored `medium`, and the family catch-all
won — suggesting registration-order or first-match rather than specificity ordering. A fallback
should lose every tie it participates in, by construction.

Related: `medium` confidence is reported for a verdict refutable from data already in memory.
Confidence can't carry much meaning while the discriminating field sits outside the predicate.

## Secondary finding — no cause code fits this failure

The runner-up is also wrong: `config_missing_reference` asserts "a referenced ConfigMap, Secret
or key could not be resolved", which did not happen here. `CreateContainerConfigError` is a
bucket reason covering at least:

- unresolvable ConfigMap/Secret reference, or a missing key within one
- securityContext violations (`runAsNonRoot` vs root image, invalid `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup`)
- bad `envFrom` sources
- invalid seccomp/apparmor profile references

The current code set collapses that bucket to its first member, so even after a precedence fix
this pod would receive a confidently-worded wrong explanation. It needs a distinct code —
`security_context_violation` or similar — discriminated on the waiting message.

## Suggested fix

- Gate `image_pull_*` on `waiting.reason ∈ {ErrImagePull, ImagePullBackOff, ImageInspectError,
  InvalidImageName, RegistryUnavailable}`; never on `CreateContainerConfigError`.
- Treat a successful `Pulled` event as a hard veto on the entire pull family.
- Make precedence explicit and specificity-ordered: fallbacks rank last, and a rule contradicted
  by the waiting reason is dropped rather than merely outranked.
- Split `CreateContainerConfigError` into its real members.

## Unrelated usability note

Running against an unreachable cluster (stale credentials — in my case a kubeconfig still pointed
at a GKE context with an expired token) surfaces a raw client-go fatal before the tool's own
error:

```
F0803 17:01:50.175523 12453 cred.go:145] print credential failed with error: ...
error: get pod default/...: Get "https://...": getting credentials: exec:
executable gke-gcloud-auth-plugin failed with exit code 1
```

Exit code is 1, which matches the documented contract. But since wrong-context/expired-credential
is probably the most common operator mistake with a tool like this, catching it and printing
something like `cannot reach cluster <server>: credentials failed — check your context/kubeconfig`
would read better than leaking client-go internals. Low priority.

title: image_pull_other: explanation omits DNS resolution failure
body:
`image_pull_other` names "a network timeout, a TLS/proxy problem, or a registry rate limit or
quota" as the typical causes. It omits name resolution — an unresolvable registry hostname, which
is a common enough case to be worth calling out.

The classification is right: `image_pull_other` is the correct bucket for this. Wording only.

## Reproduce

crashcause `v0.1.1`, k3d/k3s single node, `darwin/arm64`.

```
kubectl run dnscheck --image=no-such-registry.invalid/foo/bar:latest --restart=Never
kubectl crashcause inspect dnscheck
```

## Actual

```
image_pull_other (medium confidence)

  The kubelet could not pull the image for container "app", and the registry error is neither an
  authorization failure nor a missing image. Typical causes are a network timeout, a TLS/proxy
  problem, or a registry rate limit or quota.
```

None of the three named causes applies — the host simply does not resolve.

## The discriminator is in the kubelet message

```
Failed to pull image "no-such-registry.invalid/foo/bar:latest": failed to pull and unpack image
"...": failed to resolve reference "...": failed to do request:
Head "https://no-such-registry.invalid/v2/foo/bar/manifests/latest":
dial tcp: lookup no-such-registry.invalid: no such host
```

Note `inspect`'s own evidence line truncates before reaching `dial tcp: ... no such host`, so the
deciding text isn't visible in the report even though it's present in the event.

## Suggestion

Either add "the registry hostname does not resolve" to the cause list, or split out a dedicated
sub-case keyed on `no such host` / `server misbehaving` / `i/o timeout`. If the former, it may
also be worth keeping enough of the message tail in the evidence line for the reader to tell
which of the listed causes actually applied.
